Messages.Author: Phoenix
Messages.Body:
I've been wondering this for while now and I suppose I'm not the only one.
 
Though I understand the more basic Deck strats such as Bleed, Vote etc. I'm confused as to other possible deck themes. I got a list of them from www.vekn.nu and added comments. Someone please fill in the gaps and correct were nessecary.
 
Bleed: Well duh. Deck based on bleeding. Lots of bleed cards. Often used together with Stealth.
Bounce: Redirecting bleeds to your prey (or someone else) with cards like Deflection and Telepathic Misdirection. Almost all decks have some Bleed Bounce.
Discipline: Deck based on a single discipline. Usually almost only weenies that have that Discipline, from many different clans.
Module: A standard set of cards that can be added to any deck and is effective in itself. A Potence Module would include Torn Signpost and Immortal Grapple, just as an example. There's discipline modules or concept modules (vote, bleed etc)
Prince: Deck built around the various Camarilla princes. Decks like this take advantage of the Six Traditions (or more likely the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th). Usually one clan only, but some clans lack a lot of princes. Commonly seen with Brujah, Ventrue and Nosferatu.
Rush: Combat deck. The whole deck is built around wiping out your prey's minions or getting them into torpor. This type of deck is almost always pure weenies as you need a LOT of actions per round to get it working properly. This type of deck is a slow bleeder, as it is stuffed with cards that allow directed attacks.
Ally: Deck built around allies. It's often clan-based as almost all good allies are clanbound. Small vampires and a lot of allies and ways to get them on the table. It usually also has a lot of non-discipline combat cards, since most allies can't use a discipline. Examples are a Giovanni wraith deck or a Tzimitze War Ghoul deck.
Bloat: ....somone fill me in as I have no clue whatsoever...
Clan: A deck built around a single clan. Most decks are one clan only, since it allows you to take advantage of the clan unique locations and other masters.
Equipment: Often, but not always a combat deck. An equipment deck takes advantage of powerful equipment to get done what it wants to do. An example is a Celerity Gun deck, or a !Malkav Enchanted Marionette Bleeder.
Ranged Combat: A deck based on fighting at long range. Not to confuse with a rush deck, as this deck does pack some bleed or other actions that are desirable to block. Once the action is blocked, long range strike cards are used to damage opponents, while keeping out of the fray yourself. Common disciplines to achieve this with are Celerity and Thaumaturgy.
Stealth: Obviously this is a type of deck that you simply can't block. If it does something, it works, since you can't block it. A common application is the obvious stealth and bleed. These decks are loaded with cards that give stealth.
Vote: A vote deck relies on political actions to kill its prey and gain pool. Typically a Vote deck has such obscene amounts of votes or vote cards in it, that it can establish a "vote lock", which means that it has more votes on the table, than the other four players combines.
Attrition: Someone fill me in here. No idea what this is.
Block Denial: A deck that is based on the same concept as Stealth. It simply denies blocking, but not with stealth, but in other ways. A good example are the various Strike: Combat Ends and the action continues cards, that usually make up the bulk of decks like these. Other cards are Day operation or Daring the Dawn. Most commonly seen in combination with Votes.
Close Combat: The same as Ranged Combat, but this time it's built to fight close. Mostly used with Potence and Protean.
Intercept: Also called a Wall Deck. The idea behind it is to Intercept every action your prey does and all those directed at you, no matter the amount of stealth. Intercept decks are almost always also combat decks. It's effectiveness is very dependant on the threat of blocking rather than the block actions itself. Usually seen with Tremere or Tzimitze since both those clans have Auspex and a good combat skill to back their blocking actions with.
Preconstructed: Well, this is obviously a preconstructed deck as they are sold by White-Wolf.
Retainer: Much like an ally deck, but this time it used reatiners to do what it wants. Vampires here are not as small as with an Ally deck since Retainers are often cheap or paid from the vampires blood. Most common example is a Animalism combat deck that uses reatiners for extra damage.
Toolbox: I'm not sure, but I suppose this is a deck that can do a little bit of everything... If someone has specifics, please add them here.
Weenie: Weenie is another word for "small vampire". A weenie deck uses vampires with capacities ranging from 1 to 4. It brings out a lot of minions and creates a situation where you simply can't block all his actions. The deck makes sure to make those actions the most devastating. The most common application is a weenie bleed deck, but combat is almost as common.

Well, that's the whole list. Feel free to add and modify.
 
Phoenix

Rush a minion, celerity maneuver, Blood Sweat, Blur, Blood Sweat,
Taste of Death. Sizzle, pop, hiss - mmm, nice and crispy! :-)

definitions of attrition.

> Toolbox: I'm not sure, but I suppose this is a deck that can do a little
> bit of everything... If someone has specifics, please add them here.

Your definition is a good one.
If a deck does one thing over and over again, it is a focused deck.
If a deck does one thing, then another thing, then a third thing,
then something completely different, it's a toolbox.

The main advanteges of toolbox are unpredictability and adaptability.
Your opponents will have no idea what to expect. You also can bluff your
heart out with credibility.
The disadvantage is a lack of focus. After that big bleed, you no longer
have bleed enhancers in your hand. After a combat, you no longer have
enough combat cards for a second one.

Sorry, it must have been in my blind spot :-). To differentiate the two
deckbuilding methods, I might suggest thinking of them as seperate, given
recent debate.

Intercept Decks: As you say, solely (or mostly) designed to intercept,
mainly for the purposes of getting into combat, attacking the prey and
predator's in-game assets, rather than pool.

Wall Decks: Designed on the concept of obtaining the table win via 3VP from
ousting its first prey, and being last man standing. Deck contents can vary
to achieve that goal.

I'm thinking here of the former being about decks based around an in-game
mechanic (intercept), and the latter being decks based around a tactic for
winning the game, for which intercept is a necessary, but not exclusive,
part. Maybe its a too-subtle differentiation for most purposes, but OTOH I
couldn't ever call a Ravnos-Dominate/Draba deck an Intercept deck either.
It operates far too differently from, say, a Tzimisce Intercept deck...

Agreed that an Intercept deck is not automatically a Wall Deck. You *will*
however, need Intercept (and as such Auspex, or indeed, Chimerstry) to be a
good wall. If everyone and his sister is free to do all those +1 stealth
actions, you're not a wall deck.

It gets even worse, as was mentioned in the wall deck thread, you simply
MUST have Eagle's sight in your wall deck if you want to oust your prey,
which forces you to play Auspex. This has been debated over and over again,
but I cannot say other than that I agree with that. You simply can't get
your 3 VP's if you can't block your preys bleeds.

This is why you almost always see Tzimisce Walls, as they have Auspex, a
very good combat skill and Animalism for unlimited untaps at the same time.
Tremere, with their Thaumaturgy along with Auspex are a good second choice,
since most players are more afraid of well designd Thaumaturgy than of
Visscicitude combat. Last, but not least, Toreador can be quite a force in a
wall deck, if you give them .44's and Blur and Anneke's special is JUST the
tool you need in a Wall Deck.

To sum it up, I think that Intercept is just an Archtype, which is also part
of a Wall Deck. That deck is a deck that used Intercept/Combat (in any form
you like, but usually ranged). From that PoV I didn't miss any of the
Archtypes.

Phoenix

> find a way to increase strength. Hence the increased popularity of tha/pot.
> How is this different than finding a way of getting those "crap" cards to
> work?

Because it's a combo that requires very little setup. Plenty of
vampires have tha/pot, and since the disciplines provide complementary
effects, it's not hard to use them together. Unlike, say, trying to
get Drain Essence to work well, where you have to find a way to
survive the first round of combat, then get to the second round, and
*then* make sure that the opposing minion doesn't simply dodge, S:CE,
or Immortal Grapple you. It can be done with Thoughts Betrayed and
plenty of Apportation, but at this point you've spent a whole lot of
blood (barring Ankara on one, count 'em, one, of your vampires) to get
a pretty sucky combo off. Realistically, playing Theft in two
successive rounds of combat is a lot easier to set up, and you don't
feel as foolish if all doesn't go as planned.

> Oh wow, that did help a lot. I get hit for 7, I hit someone for 3. Yeah
